questions.stem: In Archaic Greece, a polis was best described as:
options: a religious league of cities that met each year at Delphi or Olympia
a self-governing community of citizens with its own territory, laws and gods
a province of a larger Greek kingdom, ruled by a governor sent out from Athens
a fortified hilltop used only in wartime as a refuge for the farmers
questions.explanation: The polis was the city-state: an urban centre and its hinterland whose citizens governed themselves, fought in its army and worshipped its patron gods. The acropolis was one part of a polis, and leagues such as the Delphic Amphictyony were associations of poleis, not poleis themselves.

questions.stem: Every four years Athens held the Great Panathenaia, with a procession bringing a new robe to Athena on the Acropolis. This festival shows the polis acting as a religious institution because:
options: honouring the city's patron goddess was a shared civic duty
only priests and priestesses were permitted to attend it
it was organised by the Spartans for all the Greek cities
it replaced the assembly as the city's law-making body
questions.explanation: Religion and civic life were bound together: the whole community, including women, metics and visitors in set roles, took part in honouring Athena, protector of the city. The festival was organised by Athens for its own goddess and did not replace any political institution.

questions.stem: A metic in Athens was:
options: a state-owned slave who worked in the silver mines of Laurion
a Spartan who had lost his full citizenship and settled in Attica
a free foreign resident who paid a special tax and could not own land
a citizen of the lowest property class who served as a rower in the fleet
questions.explanation: Metics were free resident foreigners: they paid the metoikion tax, needed a citizen sponsor, served in the army and fleet, and could not own land or vote without a special grant. The lowest citizen class were the thêtes, who were citizens, unlike metics.

questions.stem: An Athenian citizen woman of the early fifth century was expected to:
options: vote in the ekklesia once she had borne a son to a citizen father
buy and sell land freely in her own name without a male guardian
train in public athletics alongside other girls, as in Sparta
manage her household, and could serve the city in religious roles
questions.explanation: Athenian women had no political rights and acted at law through a male guardian (kyrios), but they ran the household and held important religious offices, such as the priestess of Athena Polias. Public athletic training for girls was a Spartan custom.

questions.stem: Compared with Athenian women, Spartan women:
options: could own land and took part in physical training
could vote in the apella and serve as ephors
were kept secluded and forbidden from going outdoors
fought as hoplites in the phalanx beside their husbands
questions.explanation: Xenophon and Plutarch describe Spartan girls exercising, and Aristotle notes that Spartan women owned much of the land, which gave them more economic power than Athenian women. They had no political rights and did not fight in the phalanx.

questions.stem: From highest to lowest, Solon's four property classes were:
options: pentakosiomedimnoi, hippeis, zeugitae, thêtes
hippeis, pentakosiomedimnoi, thêtes, zeugitae
zeugitae, hippeis, pentakosiomedimnoi, thêtes
pentakosiomedimnoi, zeugitae, hippeis, thêtes
questions.explanation: The pentakosiomedimnoi (‘500-measure men’) produced at least 500 measures a year, then came the hippeis (300), the zeugitae (200) and the thêtes below that. The names reflect wealth in produce, horses for the hippeis, and a yoke of oxen for the zeugitae.

questions.stem: By placing Athenians in four classes according to the produce of their land, Solon made political rights depend on:
options: military service rather than ownership of any property
membership of one of Cleisthenes' ten new tribes
residence in the city rather than in the countryside
wealth rather than birth into an aristocratic family
questions.explanation: Before Solon, office was dominated by the aristocratic Eupatridae; afterwards eligibility depended on measured wealth, so a newly rich man could rise. Cleisthenes' tribes came about 85 years later.

questions.stem: The helots of Sparta were:
options: foreign mercenaries hired by the kings to guard the city of Sparta
an unfree population, mostly Messenians, who farmed the Spartiates' land
free inhabitants of the towns around Laconia who did most of the crafts and trade
Spartan boys in the agoge who served the older citizens at the messes
questions.explanation: The helots belonged to the Spartan state, worked the citizens' estates and handed over a share of the produce. The free inhabitants of the surrounding towns were the perioikoi, who were free but had no say in Spartan government.

questions.stem: The perioikoi of Laconia and Messenia:
options: were Athenian settlers placed in the Peloponnese after the wars
were free and ran their own towns, but had no say in Spartan policy
were full Spartan citizens who had completed the agoge and messes
were state-owned serfs tied to the land of individual Spartiates
questions.explanation: The perioikoi (‘dwellers around’) lived in their own communities, did much of the crafts and trade that Spartiates were barred from, and fought in the Spartan army. Unlike helots they were free, but unlike Spartiates they had no political rights at Sparta.

questions.stem: Plutarch, citing Aristotle, says that the ephors declared war on the helots each year when they took office. Historians usually read this as evidence that:
options: Spartiates saw the helots as an internal enemy to be controlled by force
the helots were a foreign people from Arcadia who raided Laconia every year
the ephors were elected by the helots and answered to them
Sparta had freed the helots and enlisted them as full citizens
questions.explanation: A formal declaration of war meant that killing a helot did not bring religious pollution, which fits other evidence such as the krypteia. Helots far outnumbered Spartiates, so fear of revolt shaped Spartan society and foreign policy.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares the social structures of Athens and Sparta in the early fifth century BCE?
options: Both relied on unfree labour, but Sparta's helots outnumbered its citizens
Both gave full citizenship to the free foreigners who lived among them
Sparta allowed its women to vote, while Athens did not allow women to
Athens had a fixed hereditary citizen body, while Sparta had none
questions.explanation: Athens used chattel slaves in households, workshops and mines, while Sparta depended on a large helot population that greatly outnumbered the Spartiates. Neither city gave citizenship to resident foreigners, and women voted in neither.

questions.stem: In Archaic Greece, a tyrant was:
options: the commander of the city's fleet in times of foreign war
a man who seized sole power outside the traditional constitution
a hereditary king whose right to rule was confirmed by the Delphic oracle
an elected official who governed for one year with a council
questions.explanation: A tyrannos took power by unconstitutional means, often with popular or hoplite support against the aristocracy, as Cypselus did at Corinth. The word did not at first mean a cruel ruler; several tyrants were remembered for building and prosperity.

questions.stem: Solon's seisachtheia (‘shaking-off of burdens’) of about 594 BCE:
options: created the jury courts and the pay for jurors who served in them
expelled the tyrant Hippias and restored the archons to their office
cancelled debts secured on land or person and freed those enslaved for debt
divided the land of the aristocrats equally among all the citizens of Athens
questions.explanation: The seisachtheia removed the markers of debt from mortgaged land, freed Athenians enslaved for debt and banned loans secured on a person's body. Solon refused to redistribute land, which disappointed the poor; jury pay came under Pericles.

questions.stem: Which reform of Solon did most to give the thêtes a voice in Athenian government?
options: the admission of the thêtes to the office of eponymous archon
pay for every citizen who attended a meeting of the ekklesia
the creation of the boule of 500 chosen by lot from the demes
the right of appeal to the heliaea, a court of the citizen body
questions.explanation: Solon confirmed the thêtes' place in the ekklesia and allowed appeals from magistrates to the heliaea, so ordinary citizens could judge the decisions of officials. The thêtes never formally gained the archonship in this period, assembly pay came around 400 BCE, and the boule of 500 was Cleisthenes' creation.

questions.stem: According to Plutarch, Solon encouraged trade and industry by:
options: founding colonies in Sicily and Italy to buy grain on behalf of the state
forbidding sons to work at any trade other than farming their father's land
banning the export of produce other than olive oil and attracting craftsmen
fixing the price of grain and paying farmers from the state treasury
questions.explanation: Plutarch reports that Solon allowed only olive oil to be exported, offered citizenship to craftsmen who settled in Athens, and freed a son from supporting a father who had not taught him a trade. Each measure pushed Athens towards crafts and commerce rather than relying on scarce farmland.

questions.stem: Solon refused to redistribute land or to make himself tyrant. One consequence of his reforms was that:
options: rich and poor both remained dissatisfied, and faction helped Pisistratus rise
the aristocratic families lost all of their land and left Athens to live in Sparta
the thêtes took control of the archonship and expelled the Eupatridae
Athens remained peaceful and free of faction for the next century
questions.explanation: Solon's compromise left the wealthy resentful of debt cancellation and the poor disappointed that land was not shared out. The regional factions that followed, led by Lycurgus, Megacles and Pisistratus, opened the way for tyranny.

questions.stem: Thucydides says that the Pisistratid tyrants left the laws of Athens as they were. Ancient writers present Pisistratus's rule as relatively mild mainly because he:
options: handed power to the Spartans, who governed Athens through two ephors
gave every citizen an equal share of the land of the exiled aristocrats
kept the existing laws and offices but made sure his supporters held them
abolished the archonship and ruled directly through a council of nobles
questions.explanation: Pisistratus kept Solon's laws and the archonship, ensuring his own men held office, while lending money to farmers, appointing travelling judges and sponsoring festivals and building. Sparta helped end the tyranny rather than run it.

questions.stem: The tyranny at Athens finally ended in 510 BCE when:
options: the Persians recalled Hippias to serve as satrap of Sardis
a Spartan army under Cleomenes forced Hippias to leave Athens
Harmodius and Aristogeiton assassinated the tyrant Hippias
Cleisthenes was elected archon and dismissed the tyrant's guard
questions.explanation: Harmodius and Aristogeiton killed Hipparchus, Hippias's brother, in 514 BCE, and Hippias ruled more harshly until the Spartans expelled him in 510. Thucydides points out that many Athenians wrongly believed the tyrannicides had killed the ruling tyrant.

questions.stem: Cleisthenes built each of his ten tribes from three trittyes, one from the city, one from the coast and one from the inland. The main purpose was to:
options: give the city district permanent control of both the boule and the assembly
separate the hoplites from the thêtes in the army and the fleet
mix citizens of different regions and weaken aristocratic local power
keep each aristocratic family together within a single tribe
questions.explanation: Combining three regions in every tribe cut across the local loyalties that aristocrats had used, as in the factions of the Plain, Coast and Hill. It spread political influence evenly across Attica rather than favouring the city.

questions.stem: Under Cleisthenes' reforms, the boule of 500 was made up of:
options: one hundred men from each of the old four tribes
the ten generals and their elected deputies
fifty citizens from each of the ten tribes
former archons who served on it for life
questions.explanation: The boule drew 50 members from each of the ten tribes, filled from the demes, and prepared business for the ekklesia. Former archons served for life on the Areopagus, and the earlier council attributed to Solon was 400 strong.

questions.stem: When ostracism was held in Athens, the man who received the most votes was:
options: fined and barred from holding any office again for his lifetime
sold into slavery and his property given to the treasury of Athena
exiled for ten years but kept his property and his citizenship
put to death after a trial in front of the court of the heliaea
questions.explanation: Ostracism removed a man thought too powerful or dangerous without a trial, but it was not a criminal penalty: his property was not confiscated and he could return after ten years. Citizens scratched names on ostraka, broken pieces of pottery.

questions.stem: Archaeologists found 190 ostraka bearing the name of Themistocles, written in only a few different hands. The most likely explanation is that:
options: his opponents prepared ballots in advance to hand out to voters
Themistocles wrote them himself to prove he was popular
the ostraka were practice pieces from a school for scribes
only a few citizens could vote in an ostracism at that time
questions.explanation: So many ostraka written by a few hands, apparently never used, point to an organised campaign that prepared ballots for distribution. The find also shows that literacy may have varied among voters and that ostracism could be manipulated.

questions.stem: In 462/1 BCE, the reforms of Ephialtes:
options: made the zeugitae and thêtes eligible to sit on the Areopagus at once
restored to the Areopagus the powers lost under Cleisthenes
took most powers from the Areopagus, leaving it trials for homicide
created ostracism and used it first against the friends of tyrants
questions.explanation: Ephialtes transferred the Areopagus's broad supervisory and judicial powers to the boule, the ekklesia and the popular courts, leaving it mainly homicide and some religious cases. Ostracism dates from Cleisthenes' time, and the zeugitae became eligible for the archonship only in 457.

questions.stem: Sparta's dual monarchy meant that:
options: the king was elected each year by the apella from two candidates
the ephors chose a new king whenever the old one lost a battle
two kings, from the Agiad and Eurypontid families, ruled at the same time
one king ruled in Sparta itself while the other governed the towns of the perioikoi
questions.explanation: Sparta had two hereditary kings from two royal houses, who led the army and held religious duties. They were not elected, though the ephors could put them on trial.

questions.stem: The Spartan gerousia was:
options: a council of 28 elders over 60, with the two kings
the assembly of all Spartiates over the age of 30
a board of five officials elected for a single year
the officers who trained boys in the agoge
questions.explanation: The gerousia had 28 members aged over 60, elected for life, plus the two kings; it prepared business for the apella and acted as the highest court. The five annual officials were the ephors, and the assembly was the apella.

questions.stem: The five ephors of Sparta were:
options: officials elected annually by the apella who could supervise the kings
hereditary priests of Apollo who interpreted the oracles from Delphi
the generals chosen to command the army whenever the kings were absent
members of the gerousia chosen by lot to judge cases involving helots
questions.explanation: Any Spartiate could be elected ephor for a year, and the ephors oversaw the agoge, foreign envoys and even the kings, exchanging oaths with them each month. Their power balanced the kings and the gerousia.

questions.stem: Plutarch records a rider to the Great Rhetra stating that ‘if the people choose crookedly, the elders and kings shall set it aside’. This rider:
options: gave the helots a right of appeal to the kings against their masters
limited the apella's power by letting the gerousia and kings overrule it
gave the apella the right to remove kings who governed against the law
allowed the ephors to dissolve the gerousia if it refused to meet
questions.explanation: The apella voted by shouting on proposals put to it, and the rider let the elders and kings reject decisions they thought wrong. It shows that Sparta's assembly had real but limited power, with the gerousia acting as a check.

questions.stem: Plutarch begins his Life of Lycurgus by saying that nothing can be said about the lawgiver that is not disputed. Many historians therefore:
options: accept every detail of Plutarch's account as written in Lycurgus's lifetime
reject all evidence that Sparta had a gerousia, ephors or the agoge
date Lycurgus's reforms precisely to the year of the first Olympiad
treat the Spartan system as developing over time, not one man's creation
questions.explanation: Plutarch wrote centuries later and admits his sources conflict, so many historians see the ‘Lycurgan’ system as reforms built up over time, possibly linked to the Messenian wars. The institutions themselves are well attested, even if the lawgiver is uncertain.

questions.stem: A Greek colony (apoikia) was usually:
options: a military fort that paid tribute in silver to the mother city every year
an independent polis with religious and family ties to its mother city
a province governed by magistrates sent out each year from the mother city
a trading post with no citizens that was abandoned at the end of each season
questions.explanation: Colonists, led by a founder (oikist) and often guided by Delphi, set up a new self-governing polis that shared the cults and customs of its mother city. Colonies were not ruled from the mother city, and some, like Corcyra, later quarrelled with it.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a colony and its mother city is correct?
options: Syracuse – Corinth
Taras – Athens
Byzantium – Sparta
Cyrene – Corinth
questions.explanation: Syracuse in Sicily was founded from Corinth in the late eighth century. Taras was founded by Sparta, Byzantium by Megara, and Cyrene by settlers from Thera.

questions.stem: Herodotus says that after years of drought, Thera sent men chosen from its families to found Cyrene, and drove them off when they tried to come home. This account suggests that colonisation:
options: could be forced on settlers by a community under pressure
was always the free choice of adventurous young aristocrats
was organised by the Egyptian pharaoh to settle Libya
was only possible for cities that had already become tyrannies
questions.explanation: The story shows a community under stress compelling some of its members to leave and refusing to take them back, so colonisation was not always voluntary. Herodotus also reports the role of the Delphic oracle in the foundation.

questions.stem: In 483/2 BCE, after a rich new vein of silver was found at Laurion, Themistocles persuaded the Athenians to:
options: spend the silver on building a large fleet of triremes
share the silver equally among all the citizens of Athens
pay the silver to Persia as tribute to prevent an invasion
build the Long Walls between the city and the Piraeus
questions.explanation: Herodotus says the Athenians had planned to share the windfall but Themistocles convinced them to build ships, officially for the war with Aegina. The fleet proved decisive at Salamis, and the Long Walls were built decades later.

questions.stem: Why did the growth of Athenian naval power strengthen the political position of the thêtes?
options: the thêtes paid for the new triremes from their own wealth and so earned office
only the thêtes could be elected generals after Themistocles' naval law
the fleet's victories made the thêtes richer than the pentakosiomedimnoi
the fleet relied on the poorer citizens as rowers, making their service vital
questions.explanation: Each trireme needed about 170 rowers, mostly drawn from the thêtes, so the city's security came to depend on its poorest citizens. Ancient writers linked this to the growing power of the ordinary citizen in the democracy; the wealthy, not the thêtes, paid for ships.

questions.stem: During the Ionian Revolt, Athens sent 20 ships to help the Ionians, who joined in burning Sardis in 498 BCE. According to Herodotus, the consequence for Athens was that:
options: Sparta expelled Athens from the Peloponnesian League for breaking the peace
the Ionians made Athens the leader of a new league against the Persians
Persia paid Athens to withdraw its ships and stay out of the revolt
Darius vowed to punish Athens, which helped lead to the invasion of 490
questions.explanation: Herodotus says Darius ordered a servant to remind him three times at dinner, ‘Master, remember the Athenians’. The revolt was crushed after the naval defeat at Lade in 494, and the punitive expedition of 490 ended at Marathon.

questions.stem: At Marathon in 490 BCE, the Athenians fought with the help of the Plataeans. According to Herodotus, the Spartans:
options: fought on the left wing and lost their king in the battle
refused to send any help because Athens had burned Sardis without consulting them
sent their fleet to block the Persian ships in the Bay of Marathon
arrived after the battle, having waited for the full moon as their custom required
questions.explanation: Herodotus reports that the Spartans said religious law prevented them marching before the full moon, so they reached Attica only after the battle and viewed the Persian dead. The victory belonged to the Athenians and Plataeans under generals including Miltiades.

questions.stem: According to Herodotus, the Greek defence at Thermopylae in 480 BCE failed because:
options: a local man, Ephialtes of Trachis, showed the Persians a path around the pass
the Athenian fleet abandoned Artemisium and let the Persians land behind them
Leonidas surrendered after the Persians offered the Spartans their freedom
the Spartans ran out of food and water after three weeks of siege
questions.explanation: Herodotus says Ephialtes guided Xerxes' elite troops over the mountain path, allowing them to surround the pass. Leonidas sent most allies away and stayed with his Spartans and some others to fight to the end.

questions.stem: The Greek fleet won at Salamis in 480 BCE although it was outnumbered. The best explanation of the victory is that:
options: the narrow straits stopped the Persians using their greater numbers
the Phoenician ships deserted to the Greeks on the eve of battle
the Spartan hoplites had already defeated the Persian army on land
Xerxes had sent most of his fleet home to Persia before the battle
questions.explanation: Themistocles drew the Persian fleet into the narrow waters between Salamis and the mainland, where its numbers became a disadvantage and the heavier Greek triremes could ram effectively. The land victory at Plataea came the following year.

questions.stem: Herodotus gives the size of Xerxes' land army as 1.7 million. Most historians respond to this figure by:
options: accepting it, because Herodotus counted the troops himself at Sardis
dismissing it, because the Persians never actually invaded Greece
replacing it with the exact figure recorded in Xerxes' own inscriptions
treating it as a great exaggeration of what was still a very large army
questions.explanation: Herodotus, writing a generation later from oral sources, gives figures that could not have been supplied or fed, so historians accept a large invasion while rejecting the number. No Persian record gives an exact count.

questions.stem: The Delian League was formed in 478/7 BCE, with Athens as its leader, mainly because:
options: the Ionian Greeks wanted protection and revenge against Persia
Sparta had asked Athens to defend the Peloponnese from Argos
Persia had agreed to pay Athens to keep peace in the Aegean
the Athenians wanted a fleet to attack Corinth and Megara
questions.explanation: After the Spartan regent Pausanias offended the allies, the Ionian and island Greeks turned to Athens to lead a league to free the Greeks of Asia and punish Persia. Members contributed ships or money, assessed by Aristides, to a treasury on Delos.

questions.stem: Thucydides describes Naxos, in about 470 BCE, as the first allied city to be ‘enslaved’ against established practice. He is referring to:
options: Athens forcing Naxos back into the league after it tried to leave
Persia conquering Naxos and selling its citizens into slavery
Sparta seizing Naxos from the Delian League during a truce
the Naxians enslaving the citizens of a neighbouring island
questions.explanation: Naxos tried to leave the league and was besieged and forced back into subjection, a step towards the Athenian empire, followed by Thasos in 465. Thucydides treats this as a turning point in Athens' relations with its allies.

questions.stem: In the Peloponnesian League led by Sparta, the allies:
options: paid an annual tribute to Sparta assessed by the ephors
elected Sparta's kings at a congress held at Corinth
gave up their armies and were defended by Spartan hoplites
kept their own governments but agreed to follow Sparta in war
questions.explanation: The League was a set of alliances in which members stayed autonomous but swore to have the same friends and enemies as Sparta, and later met in congress. Unlike the Delian League, it involved no regular tribute.

questions.stem: Sparta's conquest of Messenia in the eighth and seventh centuries BCE was significant because it:
options: ended Sparta's wars, allowing it to disband its army for most of a century
gave Spartiates land and helot labour but created a lasting fear of revolt
gave Sparta its first sea port and made it the leading naval power of Greece
united all the Peloponnesian cities in a league of equals without Sparta
questions.explanation: Conquered Messenians became helots, freeing Spartiates from farming to train as full-time hoplites, but the danger of revolt, shown in the great uprising after the earthquake of about 464, shaped Spartan society. The poems of Tyrtaeus reflect the Second Messenian War.

questions.stem: During the helot revolt after the earthquake of about 464 BCE, Sparta sent home the Athenian force under Cimon that had come to help at Ithome. According to Thucydides, the Spartans did this because:
options: Cimon had been ostracised before he arrived at Ithome
the helots had surrendered before the Athenians arrived
they feared the Athenians' boldness and revolutionary spirit
the Athenians had secretly allied with the Persian king
questions.explanation: Thucydides says the Spartans feared the Athenians might side with the rebels and sent them away alone of all the allies. The insult discredited Cimon, who was then ostracised, and Athens broke its alliance with Sparta.
